API routes::Authentication and authoriza.summary: Authenticate users and authorize their actions at the data boundary. Centralize session checks in a data access layer and reuse them from pages, Server Functions, and Route Handlers.
API routes::Authentication and authoriza.explanation: Authentication establishes identity, while authorization determines whether that identity may access a route or perform an operation. Centralize session verification in a data access layer, then call it from pages, Server Functions, and Route Handlers; perform permission checks close to the data access or mutation and return only the data the caller needs.

example.title: Protect a page through the data access layer
example.explanation: The page calls the shared session check before rendering protected content.

useCases.title: Protect rendered pages
useCases.scenario: A dashboard page must be visible only to signed-in users.

useCases.title: Authorize mutations
useCases.scenario: A Server Function changes account or application data.

useCases.title: Secure Route Handlers
useCases.scenario: An HTTP endpoint serves private records or performs a protected operation.

interview.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and where should checks live?
interview.answer: Authentication confirms who the user is; authorization decides what that user may access or do. The recommended design centralizes session and authorization logic in a data access layer and reuses it at data boundaries.
interview.followUp: Why is a page-level check insufficient? Because requests can directly reach Server Functions and Route Handlers, so those entry points must perform their own checks.

interview.question: How should a data access layer protect data requests?
interview.answer: Create a data access layer that verifies the session when application code requests data. It should reject or redirect unauthenticated users and return the user information needed for subsequent authorization decisions.
interview.followUp: How should the layer limit exposure? Return a DTO with only the fields required by the caller rather than the complete database record.

interview.question: How do you secure Route Handlers and Server Functions?
interview.answer: Treat Route Handlers as public API endpoints and verify whether the current user is allowed to access each one. Apply the same principle to Server Functions, especially before mutations.
interview.followUp: What additional boundary should be protected? Any operation that changes data should independently validate both the session and the requested permission.

keyPoints: Use one data access layer as the common home for data retrieval and authorization rules.
Give the layer a reusable session-verification function and invoke it before protected data operations.
The shared check must establish that the session is valid before returning identity information.
Reuse the session check across page data requests, Server Functions, and Route Handlers instead of relying on a single UI gate.
Authorization must evaluate the user's permission for the particular handler, not merely the existence of a session.
Shape responses to the minimum required data to reduce accidental disclosure.
gotchas: Authentication alone is insufficient for mutations; verify the user's permission for the specific operation.
Avoid exposing complete database objects; use a data transfer object containing only required fields.

Data & caching::Cache Components.summary: Cache Components enables component- and function-level caching with use cache. Combine cacheLife for time-based freshness and cacheTag for targeted invalidation while dynamic content can stream separately.
Data & caching::Cache Components.explanation: Enable Cache Components, then place "use cache" on a route, component, or function whose result should be reused. Set its lifetime with cacheLife and attach cacheTag for later invalidation; uncached dynamic work can still stream separately.

parameters.name: profile
parameters.description: A cache profile name or configuration used to define the lifetime of cached work.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: A string identifying cached data for later invalidation.

Data & caching::Cache Components.returns: A cached route, component, or function result whose freshness and invalidation are configured by cacheLife and cacheTag.

example.title: Cache a tagged data query
example.explanation: Enables Cache Components and caches the product query with a time profile plus an invalidation tag.

useCases.title: Cache stable server work
useCases.scenario: Reuse stable database reads or rendered UI between requests.

useCases.title: Stream dynamic sections
useCases.scenario: Keep a route responsive while request-specific content resolves.

useCases.title: Invalidate by tag
useCases.scenario: Refresh related cached results after a create, update, or delete operation.

interview.question: How do you enable and use Cache Components?
interview.answer: Cache Components provides component- and function-level caching. Enable cacheComponents, mark the desired scope with use cache, and use cacheLife to control its lifetime.
interview.followUp: How can a mutation invalidate cached work? Attach cacheTag inside the cached scope, then call updateTag or revalidateTag according to the required invalidation behavior.

interview.question: What roles do cacheLife and cacheTag play?
interview.answer: cacheLife controls time-based freshness using a cache profile, while cacheTag gives cached work an application-defined label. A mutation can invalidate that label with updateTag or revalidateTag.
interview.followUp: Why are tags useful for data that changes before its time profile expires? They provide targeted on-demand invalidation without shortening the lifetime of unrelated cached entries.

interview.question: How does caching coexist with streaming dynamic content?
interview.answer: Cache Components can combine static, cached, and dynamic content in one route. The static shell can be served immediately, while dynamic content streams when it is ready.
interview.followUp: What should be cached? Put stable data or UI in use cache scopes and leave request-dependent work outside them so it remains dynamic.

keyPoints: The feature lets you cache at component or function granularity instead of treating only an entire route as the caching unit.
Apply use cache to a route, component, or function to cache its returned work.
A file-level directive covers every export, while an inline directive limits caching to one function or component.
Use cacheLife within each cached scope to state how long its result remains valid.
Tag cached data and invalidate it after writes with the API matching the desired mutation semantics.
gotchas: A cached scope should declare its cache lifetime explicitly with cacheLife rather than relying on surrounding or default behavior.
Cache freshness and invalidation apply across the client and server layers, so their policies should be chosen together.
A fetch placed inside a use cache scope is cached automatically; do not assume legacy fetch cache options are still required.

Data & caching::cacheLife and cacheTag.summary: Use cacheLife to define how long cached data remains valid and cacheTag to group cached entries for on-demand invalidation. Both APIs are used inside a use cache scope.
Data & caching::cacheLife and cacheTag.explanation: Place cacheLife and cacheTag inside a use cache scope. cacheLife selects a named freshness profile or accepts custom timing, controlling when the cached result is revalidated or expires; cacheTag associates the result with one or more tags that can later be invalidated with updateTag or revalidateTag.

parameters.name: profile
parameters.description: A named cache-life profile or a custom configuration object for the cached entry's lifetime.

parameters.name: tags
parameters.description: One or more strings identifying related cached data.

Data & caching::cacheLife and cacheTag.returns: cacheLife and cacheTag configure the current use cache scope; they do not return the cached value.

example.title: Cache data by lifetime and tag
example.explanation: This cached function keeps product data fresh according to the hours profile and associates it with the products tag for later invalidation.

useCases.title: Time-based freshness
useCases.scenario: Data with a predictable refresh interval, such as hourly metrics.

useCases.title: Mutation-driven invalidation
useCases.scenario: A product or CMS record that must be refreshed after an edit.

useCases.title: Invalidate related content
useCases.scenario: Several cached functions or components representing one domain entity.

keyPoints: Use cacheLife to choose how long a cached function or component remains valid before time-based revalidation.
Pass a named profile such as hours, or provide a custom cache-life configuration when the built-in profiles do not fit.
Attach one or more meaningful tags to cached data so a later mutation or administrative action can invalidate related entries.
Call cacheTag within the function or component marked with use cache.
Choose updateTag when an immediate fresh result is needed after a mutation, or revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate behavior.
gotchas: Both APIs must be called within a use cache scope; they configure the cached function or component rather than arbitrary uncached code.

Data & caching::Fetch caching.summary: In Next.js 16+, Cache Components makes server data fetching dynamic by default. Use `use cache` to create explicit cached boundaries, with `cacheLife` for lifetime and `cacheTag` for invalidation.
Data & caching::Fetch caching.explanation: With Cache Components enabled, server fetches are dynamic unless they execute inside a `use cache` scope. Mark an async function or component with `use cache`; Next.js then caches its return value, while `cacheLife` controls freshness and `cacheTag` can support invalidation. Request-specific APIs such as cookies or headers require private caching instead.
Data & caching::Fetch caching.returns: The cached return value of the marked async function or component.

example.title: Cache a fetched data view
example.explanation: The component's result and the fetch performed inside its cache scope are cached with the selected lifetime.

useCases.title: Data-level caching
useCases.scenario: Cache a reusable async data function so repeated renders can reuse its result.

useCases.title: UI-level caching
useCases.scenario: Cache a page or component while leaving other route content request-time dynamic.

useCases.title: Mixed static and dynamic rendering
useCases.scenario: Render a fast shell and stream uncached request-dependent content.

interview.question: How does fetch caching change when Cache Components is enabled?
interview.answer: With Cache Components, fetches are dynamic by default. A `use cache` directive creates an explicit cache scope, and fetches inside that scope are cached automatically; `cacheLife` replaces fetch-level revalidation settings.
interview.followUp: How would you cache data that depends on the current request? Use `use cache: private` when the function reads APIs such as `cookies()` or `headers()`, rather than sharing it through ordinary cached output.

interview.question: Where can `use cache` be applied?
interview.answer: The directive can be applied at data level to an async function that fetches or computes data, or at UI level to a component or page. In either case, Next.js caches the return value of the marked function or component.
interview.followUp: Why might data-level caching be preferable? It limits the cached boundary to reusable data instead of caching an entire rendered component, while preserving the same explicit model.

interview.question: What boundary does Cache Components introduce?
interview.answer: `cacheComponents: true` enables Cache Components, and `partialPrefetching: true` is configured with it. The model lets a route combine cached output with request-time dynamic content, producing a static shell while dynamic content streams.
interview.followUp: What replaced route segment settings such as `dynamic`, `revalidate`, and `fetchCache`? Use `use cache` together with `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` for explicit caching and invalidation.

keyPoints: `use cache` is the explicit mechanism for caching an async function's or component's returned value.
Caching can be placed around data-producing functions or around a complete UI component or page.
A fetch does not need its own cache option when it runs inside a `use cache` scope.
gotchas: Do not assume a server fetch is cached when Cache Components is enabled; place it inside a `use cache` scope.
The older fetch cache modes do not by themselves define the Cache Components boundary; wrap intended cached work with `use cache`.

Data & caching::Revalidation and invalid.summary: Next.js provides deliberate cache refresh controls: updateTag for immediate read-your-own-writes, revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate invalidation, and refresh for rerunning the current route without invalidating cached data.
Data & caching::Revalidation and invalid.explanation: Next.js offers distinct invalidation behavior: updateTag expires tagged data and makes the next read wait for fresh content, while revalidateTag marks it stale and refreshes it in the background when requested. refresh only reruns the current route's dynamic work and leaves cached entries untouched.

parameters.name: tag for updateTag
parameters.description: Cache tag identifying entries to expire immediately; available to Server Actions.

parameters.name: tag for revalidateTag
parameters.description: Cache tag whose entries become stale.

parameters.name: profile
parameters.description: Cache-life profile controlling stale-while-revalidate behavior.

Data & caching::Revalidation and invalid.returns: The page documents these APIs as cache invalidation and route-refresh functions; no distinct return values are specified.

example.title: Invalidate tagged data after a write
example.explanation: Use updateTag after a mutation when the current user must immediately see fresh tagged data; use revalidateTag with a cache profile when stale-while-revalidate is acceptable.

useCases.title: Immediate post-mutation freshness
useCases.scenario: A Server Action changes a record and the submitting user must immediately see the saved value.

useCases.title: Background refresh for shared content
useCases.scenario: A webhook or Route Handler changes content and brief staleness is acceptable.

useCases.title: Refresh dynamic route data
useCases.scenario: A mutation affects dynamic, uncached route work rather than tagged cache entries.

interview.question: When should updateTag be preferred over revalidateTag?
interview.answer: updateTag immediately expires data associated with a tag and gives read-your-own-writes behavior: the next read waits for fresh data. Use it in a Server Action after a mutation when the user must see the change immediately.
interview.followUp: How would you invalidate from a webhook? Use revalidateTag with a cache-life profile because updateTag is Server Actions-only.

interview.question: What behavior does revalidateTag provide?
interview.answer: revalidateTag marks tagged entries stale and uses stale-while-revalidate behavior. A request can receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background, so it suits content where a short delay is acceptable.
interview.followUp: What does the second argument do? It supplies the cache-life profile that controls how long stale content may be served.

interview.question: How does refresh differ from cache invalidation?
interview.answer: refresh refreshes the client router from a Server Action and reruns dynamic work for the current route. It does not invalidate cached entries, so use tag invalidation separately when cached reads changed.
interview.followUp: What should be used for a changed cached read? Tag that read and call updateTag for immediate freshness or revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate behavior.

keyPoints: Revalidation updates cached data while allowing an application to keep serving fast responses.
Use on-demand APIs when a write changes data and the related cache must be refreshed deliberately.
updateTag is designed for mutations whose result must be visible to the user in the same interaction.
revalidateTag provides stale-while-revalidate behavior rather than blocking every request for fresh data.
Only Server Actions can call updateTag; other invalidation contexts need a different API.
refresh updates the current route's client view without purging its cached data.
gotchas: The second argument to revalidateTag is required in Next.js 16; the one-argument form is deprecated and produces a TypeScript error.

Learning module::Next.js 16 learning mod.summary: Next.js 16 lets a route combine prerendered UI, cached data or components, and request-time content. The use cache directive controls cacheable functions and components, while Partial Prerendering provides a static shell for fast initial loads.
Learning module::Next.js 16 learning mod.explanation: Next.js 16 can combine prerendered UI, cached components or data, and request-specific content in one route. Mark an async function or component with use cache, then use cacheLife or cacheTag when the cache needs explicit lifetime or invalidation behavior; uncached work remains request-time and surrounding static or cached UI can still be prerendered.

example.title: Cache a page and its data
example.explanation: The directive places the component and its asynchronous result in a cacheable scope, allowing the rendered product UI to be reused.

useCases.title: Data-level caching
useCases.scenario: Cache a product lookup or other repeatable asynchronous computation independently of the page that uses it.

useCases.title: UI-level caching
useCases.scenario: Cache a complete blog-post list or page UI while leaving personalized content dynamic.

useCases.title: Mixed static and dynamic pages
useCases.scenario: Deliver a fast shell immediately while slower request-specific sections resolve progressively.

interview.question: How does Next.js 16 divide static and dynamic rendering?
interview.answer: The boundary is at the component level rather than necessarily the route level. A page can therefore contain a static shell, cached sections, and dynamic content that streams at request time.
interview.followUp: How can a cached result be invalidated selectively? Use cache tags with cacheTag, then revalidate the relevant tag instead of invalidating the whole deployment.

interview.question: What does use cache cache?
interview.answer: The use cache directive caches the return value of an asynchronous function or component. It supports data-level caching for a fetcher and UI-level caching for a complete component or page.
interview.followUp: What happens around uncached request-time work? Next.js can prerender the static or cached UI surrounding that work and stream the dynamic result later.

interview.question: What is Partial Prerendering in the Cache Components model?
interview.answer: Partial Prerendering creates a static shell for the initial response and includes an RSC Payload for client navigation. With Cache Components, this model is the default rendering approach described by the documentation.
interview.followUp: How can navigation avoid waiting for the actual click? Prefetch a cached UI using Link's prefetch behavior or the prefetch function.

keyPoints: Static and dynamic behavior can coexist within one route because the decision boundary is a component, not the entire route.
Caching can target either a data-producing function or a UI-producing component.
Caching remains available inside a route that otherwise renders dynamically.

Mutations::Cookies and sessions.summary: Use the cookies API in Server Actions to read, set, or delete session cookies. Keep request-dependent cookie access outside cached scopes and authorize mutations with server-side session data.
Mutations::Cookies and sessions.explanation: In a Server Action, obtain the request's cookie store with the asynchronous cookies API, then read, set, or delete cookie values. Cookie mutations belong in explicit server-side mutation contexts rather than rendering; after a mutation, Next.js re-renders the current page and layouts so the interface can observe the new value. Cached scopes must receive request-derived cookie values as arguments instead of reading cookies directly.

example.title: Create and delete a session cookie
example.explanation: Use these server-side mutations to create or remove a session cookie.

useCases.title: Set a session identifier after authenticating a user.
useCases.scenario: Sign-in

useCases.title: Delete the session cookie and invalidate the associated server session.
useCases.scenario: Sign-out

useCases.title: Re-read the session inside the action before changing protected data.
useCases.scenario: Authenticated mutation

interview.question: How do you manage a session cookie in a mutation?
interview.answer: Use the cookies API in a Server Action to get, set, or delete cookies. A session cookie can carry an identifier that server code uses to associate the request with session state.
interview.followUp: How should cached code use authentication state? Read cookies outside the cached scope and pass the resolved value as an argument, because cached functions cannot access request-time cookies directly.

interview.question: What happens after a Server Action changes a cookie?
interview.answer: Setting or deleting a cookie in a Server Action makes Next.js re-render the current page and its layouts on the server. This lets the rendered UI reflect the updated cookie value.
interview.followUp: What should a logout mutation do beyond deleting the browser cookie? It should also invalidate or remove the corresponding server-side session so the identifier cannot authorize future requests.

interview.question: Can cached components read cookies directly?
interview.answer: Request-dependent APIs such as cookies cannot be called from a function marked with use cache. Resolve the request data before entering the cached function and provide only the required values as parameters.
interview.followUp: Why is this restriction useful? It prevents request-specific state from accidentally becoming part of a shared cache entry.

keyPoints: The rerender makes cookie-dependent interface state update after the mutation.
For cache-compatible code, resolve cookie data before calling a cached function and pass the result explicitly.
Caching can apply to routes, components, or functions, so cookie access must be kept outside any affected cached scope.
A mutation should obtain and validate the session on the server instead of trusting client-provided authorization state.
gotchas: Cookie writes and deletes must occur in a Server Action; do not perform them during component rendering.
Do not call cookies inside a `use cache` scope; resolve the cookie outside and pass the needed value in.

Mutations::CSRF and action security.sourceTitle: How to think about data security in Next.js
Mutations::CSRF and action security.summary: Treat every Server Function as a public POST endpoint: authenticate and authorize the caller, validate client-controlled input, and rely on Next.js's Origin-versus-host check for CSRF protection. Configure allowedOrigins when trusted proxies or deployment layers use different origins.
Mutations::CSRF and action security.explanation: A Server Function can be called through a direct POST request, so the function itself must authenticate and authorize the caller and validate every input. Next.js limits invocation to POST and checks Origin against Host or X-Forwarded-Host; configure allowedOrigins when trusted proxy or CDN origins differ from the application host.

parameters.name: action arguments
parameters.description: The action's arguments, commonly FormData from a form; treat all client-provided values as untrusted and validate them server-side.

Mutations::CSRF and action security.returns: The page describes security requirements for mutations rather than a fixed return value; an individual Server Function may return application-specific data or errors.

example.title: Secure Server Function
example.explanation: The action authenticates the caller and validates untrusted form data before performing the mutation.

useCases.title: Protect form mutations
useCases.scenario: A form creates or updates a database record.

useCases.title: Allow trusted deployment origins
useCases.scenario: A mutation is invoked through a proxy or CDN whose external host differs from the application server.

useCases.title: Enforce per-resource authorization
useCases.scenario: A sensitive operation depends on the current user and a specific resource.

interview.question: Why must Server Functions be treated like public API endpoints?
interview.answer: Server Functions are public endpoints because callers can invoke them with direct POST requests instead of using the application UI. Each function must independently verify authentication, authorization, and untrusted inputs.
interview.followUp: How should a mutation handle a user who is logged in but lacks access to a resource? It must perform an authorization check for that specific resource before mutating it.

interview.question: How does Next.js reduce CSRF risk for Server Actions?
interview.answer: Next.js permits only POST requests for Server Action invocation and compares Origin with Host or X-Forwarded-Host. A mismatch aborts the request, and trusted additional origins can be configured with serverActions.allowedOrigins.
interview.followUp: What deployment issue can require allowedOrigins? A reverse proxy or CDN may expose a different trusted origin than the application server, so that origin must be explicitly configured.

interview.question: What must be validated inside a mutation?
interview.answer: FormData, query parameters, and headers come from the client and are therefore untrusted. The action should parse and validate them on the server before using them in a mutation.
interview.followUp: Why is client-side validation insufficient? A caller can alter or omit client-generated values, so server-side validation must enforce the actual input constraints.

keyPoints: Exported Server Functions should be designed as publicly reachable endpoints, even when the normal caller is a form or UI control.
Perform identity and permission checks inside every mutation; rendering an authenticated page is not enough.
Validate form data, URL parameters, headers, and other client-controlled values on the server before using them.
The invocation method is POST-only, which helps prevent ordinary cross-site GET side effects.
A request with a mismatching Origin and host is rejected before the action runs.
gotchas: Showing a form only to authenticated users does not secure the mutation; requests can bypass the UI, so checks belong inside the Server Function.
The origin check is not an unconditional rejection for missing Origin headers; treat authentication, authorization, and input validation as mandatory defenses.
If infrastructure changes the externally visible host, configure serverActions.allowedOrigins with the trusted origins.

Mutations::Server Functions.summary: Server Functions are asynchronous server-side functions for mutations. Mark them with 'use server', invoke them from forms or client transitions, and validate plus authenticate and authorize every call.
Mutations::Server Functions.explanation: A Server Function is an asynchronous server-side function exposed to client code through a network request. Mark it with 'use server', invoke it through a form's action or formAction, or call it from client event logic via a transition; validate all inputs and authenticate and authorize every invocation before changing data.

parameters.name: formData
parameters.description: The submitted form fields when invoked through a form.

Mutations::Server Functions.returns: An asynchronous result from the Server Function; the page describes returned data and re-rendered UI being carried in the response.

example.title: Mutate from a form
example.explanation: The form passes its submitted FormData to an asynchronous Server Function, where input checks and security checks belong.

useCases.title: Form mutations
useCases.scenario: A user submits fields to create or update a record.

useCases.title: Event-driven mutations
useCases.scenario: A client-side interaction needs to trigger a server-side write without a traditional form.

useCases.title: Secure public actions
useCases.scenario: A mutation must enforce access rules and reject malformed input before persistence.

interview.question: What is a Server Function?
interview.answer: A Server Function is an asynchronous function executed on the server. The 'use server' directive marks it for server execution, and client code can invoke it through a network request.
interview.followUp: How should it be secured? Authenticate and authorize inside the function itself, then validate all received inputs because the endpoint is directly callable.

interview.question: How do forms invoke Server Functions?
interview.answer: A form can pass a Server Function to its action prop, and React supplies the submitted FormData when the form is submitted. A button inside the form can instead use formAction for a specific action.
interview.followUp: Can it be called without a form? Yes: client event handlers and useEffect can invoke it through a transition such as startTransition.

interview.question: What security rules apply to mutations?
interview.answer: The function should validate FormData and perform authentication and authorization before mutating storage. Rendering a form only for authenticated users does not protect the action because requests can bypass the UI.
interview.followUp: What input sources require the same treatment? Query parameters and headers are also untrusted and must be validated before use.

keyPoints: Server Functions execute on the server and must be asynchronous.
The term Server Action describes a Server Function used for an action or mutation.
The documented invocation categories are forms, plus event handlers or useEffect in Client Components.
Each public mutation must independently enforce authentication and authorization.
gotchas: Do not treat a rendered form or visible UI as a security boundary; callers can submit direct POST requests.
Validate and sanitize every value received by the function before using it.
The function must be async because client invocation crosses a network boundary.

Navigation::Navigation and prefetching.summary: Use Link for client-side navigation and automatic viewport-triggered prefetching. Dynamic routes can partially prefetch shared layouts and loading skeletons when loading.tsx is present, enabling faster transitions.
Navigation::Navigation and prefetching.explanation: Next.js uses Link for client-side navigation and automatically prefetches linked routes as they enter the viewport. For dynamic routes, it can prefetch the shared layout and loading skeleton ahead of the destination, allowing the transition to render incrementally while the remaining route data loads.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: The destination URL passed to Link; the page demonstrates route links such as /products/1.

parameters.name: prefetch
parameters.description: Optional Link setting that controls whether automatic prefetching is enabled.

Navigation::Navigation and prefetching.returns: A client-side navigation transition to the linked route; prefetching may prepare the route or its shared layout and loading UI beforehand.

example.title: Prefetch a product route
example.explanation: A visible Link lets Next.js prefetch the destination before navigation; shared layouts and loading UI can be reused during the transition.

useCases.title: Prepare likely product navigations
useCases.scenario: A product catalogue contains many detail-page links.

useCases.title: Reuse shared dashboard layouts
useCases.scenario: An app has a persistent dashboard shell and dynamic child pages.

useCases.title: Stream through a loading boundary
useCases.scenario: A dynamic page needs immediate feedback while its data arrives.

interview.question: When does Next.js prefetch a Link destination?
interview.answer: Next.js prefetches a Link destination in the background when the link enters the viewport. This prepares navigation before the user activates the link, reducing the wait for route resources.
interview.followUp: What happens for a dynamic route? The route may be skipped or partially prefetched when loading.tsx supplies a loading boundary.

interview.question: What does partial prefetching prepare for a dynamic route?
interview.answer: A shared layout can be requested before navigation together with loading skeletons. The destination then becomes incrementally renderable instead of waiting for every dynamic part.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful with many links? Shared route structure can be reused, reducing duplicate work across destinations.

interview.question: How do shared layouts improve navigation?
interview.answer: Layouts preserve shared UI across route changes, while client-side navigation updates the changing segment rather than reloading the entire document. This makes transitions feel faster and keeps persistent interface state in place.
interview.followUp: What should a developer add for dynamic content? Add loading.tsx so a partial prefetch and immediate loading experience are available.

keyPoints: Prefetching shifts route loading before the click, so navigation can begin with resources already available.
Partial prefetching can fetch reusable layouts and loading UI before the dynamic page-specific response is ready.
The framework derives its default prefetch candidates from links rendered by the application.
gotchas: Dynamic routes are not necessarily prefetched in full: without loading.tsx, prefetching may be skipped; with it, only a partial route can be prepared.
Prefetch work is scheduled and can be discarded when a link leaves the viewport, so visibility does not guarantee that every request completes.

Navigation::useRouter and useSearchParam.summary: In App Router Client Components, useSearchParams reads the current query string while useRouter performs client navigation. Copy the read-only parameters, modify the copy, and navigate with the resulting URL.
Navigation::useRouter and useSearchParam.explanation: In an App Router Client Component, useSearchParams reads the current URL query string through a read-only URLSearchParams-like object. Copy it before changing values, then use useRouter navigation such as push or replace with the resulting URL; usePathname can be composed with these hooks when page-change detection is needed.

parameters.name: useRouter()
parameters.description: No parameters.

parameters.name: useSearchParams()
parameters.description: No parameters.

Navigation::useRouter and useSearchParam.returns: useRouter() returns the Next.js router instance. useSearchParams() returns a read-only URLSearchParams interface for the current query string; in the Pages Router it may return null during prerendering.

example.title: Read and update a query parameter
example.explanation: Reads the current label with useSearchParams, copies the read-only values into URLSearchParams, then navigates with the updated query string.

useCases.title: Query-driven controls
useCases.scenario: A filter or search control needs to reflect the current query and update it without manually assembling every parameter.

useCases.title: Client navigation
useCases.scenario: A client-side action should navigate to a new route or query-string state without a full page reload.

useCases.title: Navigation event composition
useCases.scenario: A navigation-aware UI needs to respond when the pathname or query string changes.

interview.question: What is the division of responsibility between useRouter and useSearchParams?
interview.answer: useRouter performs client navigation and exposes methods such as push and replace. useSearchParams separately reads the current URL query string, replacing the old router query object in the App Router.
interview.followUp: How would you update one query value without rebuilding the whole query string? Copy searchParams with new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()), modify the copy, and pass its serialized value to router.push or router.replace.

interview.question: How should a component update a search parameter?
interview.answer: useSearchParams returns a read-only URLSearchParams-style interface, so it is suitable for reading values such as the first result from get(). To update a value, construct a mutable URLSearchParams copy.
interview.followUp: Why not call set directly on the hook result? The hook result is read-only; mutating a separate copy avoids treating the returned interface as writable.

interview.question: What rendering constraint applies to these hooks?
interview.answer: These hooks are Client Component hooks and cannot be used in Server Components. A component using useSearchParams also skips prerendering and is rendered on the client at runtime during prerendering.
interview.followUp: How can a page listen for navigation changes? Compose usePathname and useSearchParams, then react to their values in a Client Component.

keyPoints: useSearchParams reads the query string belonging to the current URL.
URLSearchParams supplies standard methods for creating and editing a copied query string.
Combine usePathname and useSearchParams when a component needs to observe page changes.
gotchas: Do not expect useRouter to provide query values; read URL search parameters with useSearchParams instead.
Do not mutate the returned search-parameter object directly; create a new URLSearchParams instance from its string representation.

Performance::Bundle analysis.summary: Analyze client and server bundles with Next.js's Turbopack Bundle Analyzer, then use module sizes and import chains to find expensive client dependencies. Remove, split, or lazy-load code to reduce what reaches the browser.
Performance::Bundle analysis.explanation: Bundle analysis exposes how much code and assets each route ships to the browser or server. Use route, environment, type, and import-chain views to locate expensive client dependencies, then remove, split, or lazy-load them so browser-free work remains server-side.
Performance::Bundle analysis.returns: An interactive local bundle-analysis view by default, or a static analysis file when `--output` is supplied.

example.title: Save a bundle analysis
example.code: npx next analyze --output
example.explanation: Runs the Turbopack bundle analyzer and writes a static analysis file instead of opening only the interactive view.

useCases.title: Find oversized client dependencies
useCases.scenario: A route ships more JavaScript than expected.

useCases.title: Compare bundle composition
useCases.scenario: An optimization needs evidence before and after a change.

useCases.title: Trace import chains
useCases.scenario: A dependency appears unexpectedly in a route.

interview.question: How do you analyze a Next.js bundle?
interview.answer: Run `npx next analyze` to inspect bundle composition. The analyzer can filter by route, switch between client and server views, and show JavaScript, CSS, JSON, and other asset sizes.
interview.followUp: How would you investigate a large client dependency? Filter to the affected route and client environment, select the module, then inspect its complete import chain to find why it is included.

interview.question: What does import tracing tell you?
interview.answer: The analyzer shows a module's size and its complete import chain. That identifies both the expensive module and the import path that caused it to enter a route's bundle.
interview.followUp: What optimization choices follow from that information? Remove an unnecessary dependency, split code, or lazy-load functionality that is not needed for the initial route.

interview.question: When would you use the output option?
interview.answer: Use `npx next analyze --output` when the analysis should be saved as a static file rather than viewed only interactively. This supports sharing results or comparing bundle sizes before and after an optimization.
interview.followUp: What should be compared? Compare the affected route's client resources and dependency contributors, while also checking that the optimization did not shift an unwanted cost elsewhere.

keyPoints: Bundle analysis evaluates the optimized output produced by combining application code with its dependencies for client and server delivery.
Next.js performs baseline bundle optimization automatically, so analysis helps identify remaining route-specific costs rather than replacing those optimizations.
The Turbopack analyzer reads the module graph and can expose precise relationships between imports and resulting bundle costs.
Narrow investigations by route, client/server environment, and asset type before evaluating a dependency's impact.
Selecting a module reveals its size and full import chain, helping locate the import responsible for shipping it.
Reducing shipped bundle size benefits loading, JavaScript execution, and Core Web Vitals.
gotchas: The Turbopack analyzer is intended for Turbopack module graphs; it is not the Webpack plugin workflow.
Do not interpret a dependency's presence alone as proof of client cost; inspect whether the module belongs to the client or server graph and trace its imports.

Performance::Images, fonts and metadata.summary: Next.js lets you define SEO and sharing metadata with static or generated APIs, while file conventions handle icons and social images. It automatically produces the relevant head elements for each page.
Performance::Images, fonts and metadata.explanation: Next.js provides a Metadata API for SEO and sharing details. Define static metadata with an exported object, compute data-dependent values with generateMetadata, or use special files for icons and social images; Next.js then creates the appropriate head tags.
Performance::Images, fonts and metadata.syntax:
export const metadata: Metadata = { ... }
export async function generateMetadata(): Promise<Metadata> { ... }

example.title: Static page metadata
example.explanation: Export a Metadata object from a server page or layout to let Next.js create the corresponding head tags.

useCases.title: Static route metadata
useCases.scenario: A page has fixed title, description, or social metadata known in source code.

useCases.title: Data-dependent metadata
useCases.scenario: A product, article, or profile page needs title and description from fetched data.

useCases.title: File-based icons and social images
useCases.scenario: A site needs favicons or share previews without manually adding link and meta tags.

useCases.title: Dynamic Open Graph images
useCases.scenario: Social previews must include runtime-generated text or imagery.

interview.question: When should you use metadata versus generateMetadata?
interview.answer: Use an exported `Metadata` object in a layout or static page when values are known at build time. Use `generateMetadata` when metadata depends on fetched or otherwise dynamic data.
interview.followUp: Where can these APIs run? They are supported only in Server Components, so client-only modules cannot export them.

interview.question: How does Next.js turn metadata declarations into HTML?
interview.answer: Next.js automatically resolves metadata and creates the relevant head tags for the page. Metadata can be supplied through configuration exports or special file conventions.
interview.followUp: Name two file conventions: `favicon.ico` for a favicon and `opengraph-image.jpg` for a static Open Graph image.

interview.question: What asset and sharing features are covered by this API?
interview.answer: The metadata API covers SEO and web shareability, including static metadata, generated metadata, favicons, and Open Graph images. Dynamic Open Graph images can also be produced with `ImageResponse`.
interview.followUp: What can ImageResponse use for the image layout? It supports JSX and CSS, including flexbox, absolute positioning, text wrapping, centering, nested images, and supported custom fonts.

keyPoints: Metadata declarations improve search presentation and how shared pages appear.
Export a static metadata object when route metadata does not need runtime data.
Use generateMetadata when metadata must be derived from fetched or changing values.
Special metadata files support favicons and Open Graph images without manually writing head markup.
Next.js combines metadata sources and emits the corresponding head elements automatically.
ImageResponse is available for programmatically generated social images using JSX and CSS.
gotchas: Do not export metadata APIs from Client Components; keep the defining page or layout as a Server Component.

Performance::next/font.summary: `next/font` optimizes and self-hosts Google or local fonts during the build. It avoids external font requests and helps prevent layout shift while keeping font assets with the deployment.
Performance::next/font.explanation: `next/font` turns font loading into a build-time operation. Import a loader from `next/font/google` or `next/font/local`, call it with options, and apply the returned `className`; Next.js self-hosts the resulting assets so browsers do not need external font requests.
Performance::next/font.returns: A font object whose generated `className` can be applied to an element.

example.title: Apply a Google font globally
example.explanation: This loads Inter through the Google font loader and applies the generated class to the application body.

useCases.title: Global application typography
useCases.scenario: Apply a consistent typeface across an App Router application by configuring the font in the root layout.

useCases.title: Privacy-conscious Google fonts
useCases.scenario: Use a supported Google family without making browser requests to Google's servers.

useCases.title: Local or custom fonts
useCases.scenario: Bundle project-owned font files as deployment assets.

interview.question: What does `next/font` optimize?
interview.answer: The loader downloads and prepares CSS and font assets during the build, then serves them with the application. This removes runtime font requests to external providers and enables self-hosting.
interview.followUp: How would you make a font available throughout an App Router application? Define it in the root layout and apply its returned class to the relevant top-level element.

interview.question: How do Google and local fonts differ in usage?
interview.answer: Use a font export from `next/font/google`, call it with the required options, and attach the returned `className` to an element. For a file you own, use `next/font/local` and specify `src`.
interview.followUp: Why might local loading be preferable? It lets the deployment serve the font from its own assets and avoids relying on a third-party font host.

interview.question: How do you apply a font globally?
interview.answer: A font is scoped to the component where its generated class is applied. To use it across pages in the App Router, configure it in the root layout and place the class on a shared ancestor such as `body`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the class is applied only to a nested component? The font affects that component's rendered subtree, not unrelated routes or ancestors.

keyPoints: The module optimizes font loading while avoiding browser requests to external font services.
Font files can be served as part of the application instead of requiring a separate font host.
The loading strategy is designed to prevent layout movement caused by late font replacement.
Google fonts are packaged into the deployment and delivered from the application's own domain.
The build produces the font-related assets alongside the application's other static resources.
gotchas: A font used in only one component does not automatically apply across the application; put it in the root layout when it should be global.
For local files, use the local loader and provide the file source rather than importing a Google font.

Performance::Static and dynamic renderin.summary: Static rendering builds or revalidates a page ahead of requests and serves its cached result. Dynamic rendering generates the page for each request, which suits personalized or frequently changing data but can be limited by slow fetches.
Performance::Static and dynamic renderin.explanation: Static rendering creates the response ahead of a request and reuses its cached result, making it suitable for shared, non-personalized data. Dynamic rendering generates content per request when the result depends on request-time information or data that cannot be cached.
Performance::Static and dynamic renderin.returns: A rendered page response, either reused from the cache or generated at request time.

example.title: A statically rendered product page
example.explanation: The revalidated fetch lets Next.js render and cache the product page ahead of requests, refreshing its data periodically.

useCases.title: Shared catalog content
useCases.scenario: A blog post or product page is shared across users and can be generated before requests.

useCases.title: Personalized dashboards
useCases.scenario: A dashboard displays user-specific information or data that must be current at request time.

useCases.title: Real-time views
useCases.scenario: A page depends on frequently updated backend data and freshness matters more than cache reuse.

keyPoints: Static rendering performs data fetching and rendering during the build, or later when cached data is revalidated.
Subsequent visitors receive the cached rendered result rather than triggering rendering for every request.
Use static rendering for pages whose content is identical or broadly shareable between users.
Dynamic rendering produces the page when the user requests it, enabling request-specific output.
Use dynamic rendering when the page must show current data instead of a previously cached result.
gotchas: A slow request-time fetch can delay the whole dynamic response.

Rendering::Metadata API.summary: Next.js Metadata API defines route metadata for SEO and web sharing. Use a static metadata object, generateMetadata for dynamic values, or metadata file conventions for assets such as Open Graph images.
Rendering::Metadata API.explanation: The Metadata API lets App Router layouts and pages export either a static Metadata object or a server-only generateMetadata function. Next.js resolves these declarations into head elements; route segments can also use special metadata files for assets such as Open Graph images.
Rendering::Metadata API.syntax:
export const metadata: Metadata = {}
export async function generateMetadata(): Promise<Metadata> {}

parameters.name: generateMetadata input
parameters.description: A Metadata object or function input containing route/data values used to compute metadata.

Rendering::Metadata API.returns: generateMetadata returns a Metadata object containing one or more metadata fields.

example.title: Generated route metadata
example.explanation: A dynamic route computes metadata from its route parameter and returns title, description, canonical, and Open Graph fields.

useCases.title: Shared layout metadata
useCases.scenario: A site-wide title template and description are shared through a root or nested layout.

useCases.title: Dynamic page metadata
useCases.scenario: A product, article, or profile page needs title and description values derived from route data.

useCases.title: File-based social and icon metadata
useCases.scenario: A page needs social preview artwork or icons served by route-aware conventions.

interview.question: When should you use metadata versus generateMetadata?
interview.answer: Use a Metadata export for fixed values in a layout or page. Use generateMetadata when values depend on route parameters or other data, and return a Metadata object.
interview.followUp: Why is this server-only? Metadata must be resolved before rendering so Next.js can place it in the initial HTML response.

interview.question: What are the two ways to define metadata?
interview.answer: Config-based metadata is declared in a layout.js or page.js file. File-based metadata uses special files in route segments, and Next.js creates the relevant head elements automatically.
interview.followUp: Name a file-based convention for social previews. opengraph-image and twitter-image are supported conventions.

interview.question: What problems does the Metadata API solve?
interview.answer: The Metadata API defines head metadata such as meta and link tags for SEO and web sharing. The Metadata object supports fields such as title, description, Open Graph data, and canonical alternatives.
interview.followUp: How can a route provide a generated social image? Use the dynamic Open Graph image file convention in the route segment.

keyPoints: Metadata can be configured in code or supplied with special files in route segments.
A static Metadata object suits values known at build or module definition time; generateMetadata handles dynamic values.
Next.js turns either configuration style into the page's appropriate head elements.
Static metadata is exported from a layout or static page.
Metadata fields can be set through either the static object or generated metadata.
gotchas: Do not export metadata declarations from Client Components; keep them in Server Components.
Use generateMetadata when metadata depends on route or fetched data rather than a fixed object.
Open Graph images can also be supplied through the file-based metadata conventions.

Rendering::Not-found handling.summary: Call `notFound()` when a route’s requested resource is absent. It terminates rendering for that segment and renders the nearest not-found UI, while adding a no-index robots directive.
Rendering::Not-found handling.explanation: In a route segment, call `notFound()` when data lookup shows that the requested resource does not exist. Next.js throws an internal 404 signal, stops rendering that segment, and selects the nearest `not-found.tsx`; the framework also marks the response as not indexable.
Rendering::Not-found handling.returns: Never returns normally; calling `notFound()` throws an internal 404 error that terminates rendering of the current route segment.

example.title: Handle a missing resource
example.explanation: Call `notFound()` when the requested resource is absent; add a nearby `not-found.tsx` to render the segment's 404 UI.

useCases.title: Missing dynamic resources
useCases.scenario: A dynamic page looks up a post, product, invoice, or user and the lookup returns no record.

useCases.title: Server-side resource validation
useCases.scenario: A server-side action or route handler validates an identifier and cannot find the referenced entity.

useCases.title: Custom segment not-found UI
useCases.scenario: A route needs a segment-specific 404 interface instead of a generic application fallback.

useCases.title: Streaming-aware existence checks
useCases.scenario: A page should preserve its shell and loading state while checking resource existence.

interview.question: How does `notFound()` handle a missing resource?
interview.answer: Call `notFound()` from the render path after determining that the requested resource is absent. It throws a framework 404 signal, stops rendering the current route segment, and renders the applicable not-found UI.
interview.followUp: What happens if the call is wrapped in `try/catch`? The catch can suppress the internal signal, so the not-found UI will not render unless the framework error is rethrown.

interview.question: How do you customize the UI?
interview.answer: Create a `not-found.tsx` file in the relevant route segment to define its UI. If that boundary is absent, Next.js uses the nearest parent boundary and ultimately its default 404 page.
interview.followUp: How can an application handle a URL that matches no route? Use the root not-found convention for unmatched URLs, or the experimental global convention for an application-wide page.

interview.question: Where can `notFound()` be invoked, and what SEO behavior does it provide?
interview.answer: The function can be used in Server Components, Server Functions, and Route Handlers. Next.js also injects a `noindex` robots meta tag so the missing-resource page is not indexed.
interview.followUp: What changes after streaming begins? The UI still renders, but the HTTP status remains 200 rather than 404.

keyPoints: Use `notFound()` to switch from normal route rendering to a 404 response and the applicable not-found interface.
The call ends processing for the segment immediately; code after the invocation is not part of the rendered result.
Missing-resource pages receive a no-index robots directive automatically.
gotchas: Do not catch the call without rethrowing the framework-controlled error, or the not-found boundary will not be reached.
A streamed response can display not-found UI while retaining HTTP status 200; before streaming, Next.js returns 404.
Invoke the function directly; adding `return` is unnecessary because the function terminates execution by throwing.

Rendering::Server and Client Components.summary: Use Server Components by default for data fetching, secrets, smaller browser bundles, and streaming. Add a 'use client' boundary only where state, event handlers, effects, or browser APIs are needed.
Rendering::Server and Client Components.explanation: In the App Router, layouts and pages are Server Components by default, so they can fetch data near its source, keep secrets server-side, reduce browser JavaScript, and stream rendered UI. Add the 'use client' directive to a module when it needs state, event handlers, lifecycle logic, or browser APIs; that directive establishes the boundary for the client module graph, including modules imported by it.

example.title: Server page with an interactive client island
example.explanation: Keep the route page on the server and isolate browser state and event handling in a small Client Component.

useCases.title: Server-first data rendering
useCases.scenario: A page loads database-backed content and renders it without browser interaction.

useCases.title: Interactive client island
useCases.scenario: A small control needs clicks, local state, or browser APIs.

useCases.title: Protected server-side access
useCases.scenario: Credentials or tokens are required while assembling a response.

interview.question: What is the default component type in the App Router, and why?
interview.answer: Next.js uses Server Components by default for layouts and pages. They render on the server, can fetch close to data sources, and their code is not sent to the browser.
interview.followUp: How do you add browser behavior? Mark a module with 'use client' before imports; that module becomes a client entry point and its imported dependency graph is included in the client graph.

interview.question: When should a component be a Client Component?
interview.answer: Use Client Components for state, event handlers, effects, or browser-only APIs. They are hydrated on the initial load and can update in the browser.
interview.followUp: How can a server-rendered route still contain interactive UI? Keep the page or layout server-side and nest a narrowly scoped Client Component where interaction is required.

interview.question: How do Server and Client Components work together?
interview.answer: The server renders Server Components into the React Server Component Payload, which includes references to Client Components and serialized props. Next.js uses that payload with client code to produce the UI and hydrate interactive parts.
interview.followUp: Can a Client Component directly import a Server Component? No; pass the Server Component through props or children so composition crosses the boundary without a client-to-server import.

keyPoints: App Router layouts and pages start as Server Components, so server rendering is the default choice.
Server Components can retrieve data and produce UI on the server before the result reaches the browser.
Server-only code is the appropriate place for credentials and other sensitive values.
Choosing server rendering for noninteractive UI helps keep the browser bundle smaller.
Client Components are the opt-in mechanism for browser interaction and browser-provided APIs.
The directive separates the server and client dependency graphs at a module boundary.

Rendering::Streaming with Suspense.summary: Use Suspense boundaries to send a route’s ready shell and fallback first, then stream slower server-rendered regions as they resolve. Sibling boundaries can complete independently, while loading.tsx provides automatic route-level streaming.
Rendering::Streaming with Suspense.explanation: Next.js can render the route shell and send it before slower work completes. Put the slow component inside a React Suspense boundary; its fallback becomes the visible placeholder, and the resolved component is streamed into that boundary independently of sibling boundaries.
Rendering::Streaming with Suspense.returns: A progressively delivered UI: the fallback is sent while suspended work is pending, followed by the resolved content.

example.title: Stream a slow component
example.explanation: The heading renders in the initial shell, while the slow Server Component is replaced by the fallback until it resolves.

useCases.title: Show the page shell before slow data
useCases.scenario: A route has a slow data request but includes headings, navigation, or controls that can render immediately.

useCases.title: Reveal independent widgets progressively
useCases.scenario: Several dashboard widgets have different response times.

useCases.title: Stream a route with loading.tsx
useCases.scenario: A dynamic route needs a route-level loading state during navigation.

interview.question: What does Suspense contribute to Next.js streaming?
interview.answer: Streaming splits server rendering into chunks and sends each chunk as it becomes ready. A Suspense boundary defines an independent point where a fallback can be sent first and the completed content can follow.
interview.followUp: How can unrelated slow regions avoid delaying one another? Put them in sibling Suspense boundaries, because components inside different boundaries resolve and stream independently.

interview.question: How does loading.tsx differ from an explicit Suspense boundary?
interview.answer: A loading.tsx file is the simplest route-level option. Next.js automatically wraps the page content in a Suspense boundary and uses the loading component as its fallback.
interview.followUp: When is a component-level boundary preferable? Use Suspense closer to runtime or uncached data access when only a region should stream and the rest of the page can render immediately.

interview.question: What is the relationship between the shell, fallback, and streamed content?
interview.answer: The static shell contains content outside the Suspense boundary and can be delivered before the suspended region resolves. The fallback provides visible UI while the slower region is pending.
interview.followUp: What triggers the initial response body? Streaming starts when a Suspense fallback renders or a component suspends under a Suspense boundary.

keyPoints: Treat every Suspense boundary as a separate delivery point for progressive rendering.
Sibling boundaries can reveal their completed UI at different times rather than waiting for one shared result.
Add loading.tsx beside a page when route-level streaming and an automatic fallback are sufficient.
The framework supplies the route-level boundary when loading.tsx is present, so no explicit wrapper is required for that case.
A streamed component can remain non-blocking, allowing surrounding page content to render without waiting.
gotchas: A stream does not begin merely because a boundary exists: the response starts when a fallback renders or a component actually suspends beneath the boundary.
Separate boundaries resolve independently, so avoid combining unrelated slow regions when they should appear progressively.

Request handling::Middleware migration t.summary: Next.js 16 deprecates the `middleware` convention and renames it to `proxy`. Migrate the root file, exported function, and affected configuration names, using the codemod when useful.
Request handling::Middleware migration t.explanation: Next.js 16 changes the request-interception convention from Middleware to Proxy. Rename the root file and exported function, then review any renamed configuration flags; Proxy uses the Node.js runtime by default.
Request handling::Middleware migration t.returns: The Proxy function can return a response such as `NextResponse.next()`, a redirect, a rewrite, or another response.

example.title: Migrate with the official codemod
example.code: npx @next/codemod@latest middleware-to-proxy .
example.explanation: Run this from the project root to rename the convention and exported function automatically.

useCases.title: Rename the request interception convention
useCases.scenario: Migrating an existing Next.js 15 project to Next.js 16

useCases.title: Run the migration codemod
useCases.scenario: Automating a mechanical migration across a project

useCases.title: Keep existing request logic
useCases.scenario: Preserving redirects, rewrites, headers, or pass-through behavior

useCases.title: Retain Middleware temporarily
useCases.scenario: Using Edge-runtime-specific Middleware behavior

interview.question: How do you migrate a Next.js 15 Middleware file?
interview.answer: In Next.js 16, rename the root `middleware.ts` file to `proxy.ts` and rename its named export from `middleware` to `proxy`. The codemod can perform both changes.
interview.followUp: What runtime does Proxy use? Proxy runs on Node.js, and the Edge runtime is unsupported; an Edge-dependent project must retain Middleware for now.

interview.question: What migration automation does Next.js provide?
interview.answer: Run `npx @next/codemod@latest middleware-to-proxy .` from the project root. It updates the file name, export name, and documented Middleware-related configuration properties.
interview.followUp: Which configuration rename might affect URL handling? `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` becomes `skipProxyUrlNormalize`.

interview.question: Does migrating to Proxy change the request-handling logic?
interview.answer: The functionality remains the same: request interception can continue to use responses such as `NextResponse.next()`. The convention and runtime model change, not the basic request-handling pattern.
interview.followUp: Can a static export use Proxy? No; Proxy requires access to the incoming request and is unsupported with static export.

keyPoints: In Next.js 16, `middleware` is the deprecated filename; use `proxy` to express the request network boundary.
The official codemod can migrate an existing Middleware convention to the Proxy convention.
Rename the root file, for example from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`.
Change a named `middleware` function to `proxy`; this keeps the exported entry point aligned with the new convention.
Update Middleware-named configuration flags, including the URL-normalization flag, to their Proxy equivalents.
Proxy has a fixed Node.js runtime rather than a configurable runtime selection.
gotchas: Proxy does not support the Edge runtime. Keep using the deprecated Middleware convention if the Edge runtime is required.
A named export still called `middleware` is deprecated; rename it to `proxy`.
Review configuration flags containing `middleware`, because their Proxy-era names may differ.

Request handling::Proxy.summary: Next.js 16 calls the former Middleware convention Proxy. A proxy.ts function runs before completion so it can make request-dependent redirects, rewrites, header changes, or direct responses.
Request handling::Proxy.explanation: Create a root-level proxy.ts file, or place it in src beside app or pages. Next.js invokes its proxy function before a request completes; the function can inspect the request and return a redirect, rewrite, modified response, or direct response. Use config.matcher to restrict invocation to selected paths. Proxy uses the Node.js runtime in Next.js 16.
Request handling::Proxy.returns: The proxy function returns a response, such as NextResponse.redirect, NextResponse.rewrite, NextResponse.next, or a direct Response.

example.title: Redirect a legacy path with Proxy
example.explanation: This redirects the selected legacy path before rendering and lets other matched requests continue.

useCases.title: Programmatic redirects
useCases.scenario: A request contains an expired or legacy URL that should move to a new route.

useCases.title: Conditional rewrites
useCases.scenario: Different incoming requests should reach different pages based on an experiment or request property.

useCases.title: Header modification
useCases.scenario: Several routes need common request or response headers before rendering.

useCases.title: Optimistic access filtering
useCases.scenario: Access decisions can be made from request metadata before a protected route renders.

interview.question: What is Proxy used for?
interview.answer: Proxy is a request-time entry point that runs before a request completes. It can inspect the incoming request and return a redirect, rewrite, header change, or direct response.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid running it on every request? Add a config.matcher pattern that includes only the routes requiring this logic.

interview.question: How do you define and place Proxy?
interview.answer: Export a function named proxy from proxy.ts or proxy.js. Put the file at the project root, or under src at the same level as app or pages, and return a response such as NextResponse.redirect or NextResponse.next().
interview.followUp: What happens if the function returns no response? Return a response explicitly; NextResponse.next() continues processing the request.

interview.question: How should route matching and simple redirects be handled?
interview.answer: Use config.matcher to filter which paths invoke Proxy. For a straightforward static redirect, use the redirects setting in next.config.ts instead of request-time Proxy logic.
interview.followUp: When is Proxy the better choice? Use it when the decision depends on incoming request properties, such as authentication or experiments.

keyPoints: In Next.js 16, the former Middleware convention is renamed Proxy; the underlying capability remains available.
Proxy is suitable for decisions that must happen before the route finishes processing.
A Proxy function can redirect, rewrite, change headers, or produce a response without rendering the target route.
Use a proxy.ts or proxy.js file at the project root, or under src when that structure is used.
Configure matcher to limit Proxy execution to selected URL patterns.
gotchas: Prefer next.config.ts redirects when the redirect is static and does not require request-specific logic.

Request handling::Proxy matchers.summary: Proxy matchers restrict Proxy execution to selected request paths. They support direct paths, arrays, regular-expression patterns, and conditional matcher objects.
Request handling::Proxy matchers.explanation: Proxy runs for every request unless its configuration narrows execution. Export `config.matcher` with a path, path array, or matcher objects to select routes; patterns can use full regular expressions and objects can additionally test locale behavior, present request values, or missing request values.
Request handling::Proxy matchers.syntax: export const config = { matcher: string | string[] | MatcherObject[] }

parameters.name: config.matcher
parameters.description: A string, an array of path strings, or an array of matcher objects describing the request paths and conditions where Proxy runs.

Request handling::Proxy matchers.returns: No return value; the configuration controls whether the exported Proxy function executes for a request.

example.title: Exclude non-page requests
example.explanation: Runs the Proxy for application pages while excluding API routes, Next.js internals, image optimization, and PNG files.

useCases.title: Route-specific request handling
useCases.scenario: Run redirects or rewrites only for selected application routes.

useCases.title: Skip non-page requests
useCases.scenario: Exclude APIs, framework internals, and static assets from broad request policy.

useCases.title: Conditional request matching
useCases.scenario: Apply policy only when headers, cookies, or query parameters meet conditions.

interview.question: How do you restrict Proxy to selected routes?
interview.answer: Export `config` beside the Proxy function and set its `matcher` property. A string selects one path, while an array selects multiple paths or matcher objects.
interview.followUp: How would you omit internal assets and APIs? Use a negative-lookahead pattern such as `/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\.png$).*)`.

interview.question: What conditional matcher features are available?
interview.answer: Use a matcher object with `source` for the path pattern. Add `locale: false` to ignore locale-based routing, `has` to require request elements, or `missing` to require their absence.
interview.followUp: How can a matcher avoid prefetched requests? Add `missing` conditions for the relevant prefetch headers.

interview.question: Can matcher patterns use regular expressions?
interview.answer: The matcher supports complex path specifications, including regular expressions. This enables exclusions with negative lookaheads and matching based on character patterns.
interview.followUp: What is the default if no matcher is exported? Proxy runs on all requests, so add an explicit matcher when broad execution is unnecessary.

keyPoints: Use `config.matcher` to limit Proxy execution to routes that need its request handling.
A single route can be selected with a string such as `'/about'`.
An array lets one Proxy cover several independent routes.
Matchers support direct paths, route patterns, arrays, and conditional object forms.
In object form, `source` defines the request-path pattern.
Set `locale` to `false` when matching should ignore locale prefixes.
Use `has` to require headers, query parameters, or cookies before Proxy runs.
Use `missing` when the route should match only if specified request elements are absent.
gotchas: Object-form matchers must be placed in an array, even when defining a single conditional matcher.
Regular expressions are powerful but easy to make too broad; test exclusions carefully so required routes are not skipped.

Routing::Dynamic routes.summary: Dynamic routes derive URL segments from runtime or build-time data. Use [segment] for one value, [...segment] for one-or-more trailing values, and [[...segment]] when the parent path should match too.
Routing::Dynamic routes.explanation: Create a dynamic route by naming a folder with square brackets, such as [slug]. Next.js supplies the captured value through the page's params prop; in a catch-all route, await that prop and use the resulting array to handle any number of path segments. Optional catch-all syntax also matches the parent path without additional segments.

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: Promise containing the values captured by dynamic route segments; values are string, string[], or undefined depending on the convention.

Routing::Dynamic routes.returns: A page component that renders the matched dynamic URL; the documentation does not specify a separate return value.

example.title: Catch-all dynamic page
example.explanation: This page renders every path below /shop and reads its segments after awaiting params.

useCases.title: Single-resource pages
useCases.scenario: A product, article, or user page has one data-backed identifier in its URL.

useCases.title: Hierarchical paths
useCases.scenario: A filesystem, documentation tree, or nested category needs arbitrary path depth.

useCases.title: Optional nested paths
useCases.scenario: One page handles both a collection root and deeper nested paths.

interview.question: How does a dynamic segment work?
interview.answer: A dynamic segment uses a bracketed folder name such as [slug]. Next.js passes its captured value to the page through params, and the route can be generated at request time or prerendered.
interview.followUp: How do you represent a route that accepts multiple trailing segments? Use [...slug], then read slug as a string array after awaiting params.

interview.question: What is a catch-all segment?
interview.answer: A catch-all segment uses [...slug] and matches one or more segments below its parent. For example, app/shop/[...slug]/page.js matches /shop/clothes and deeper paths.
interview.followUp: How can the parent path itself also match? Replace it with [[...slug]], whose value may be undefined when no trailing segment exists.

interview.question: Why must route params be awaited?
interview.answer: In the App Router, params is asynchronous, so an async page should await it before reading route values. The resulting types are string for a single segment, string[] for catch-all, and string[] or undefined for optional catch-all.
interview.followUp: What changes in a Client Component? Use React's use() to unwrap the promise rather than awaiting it directly.

keyPoints: Use a dynamic segment when URL values come from data rather than a fixed route name.
The page receives matched route values through its params prop.
A folder named [id] creates one dynamic URL segment and exposes it under the id key.
Use [...slug] when one route should consume multiple subsequent path segments.
Use [[...slug]] when the route must also match its parent path without descendants.
The parameter shape depends on the segment form: scalar, catch-all array, or optional absence.
gotchas: A normal segment produces a string, a catch-all produces a string array, and an optional catch-all can produce undefined.
Use optional catch-all syntax only when the parent URL should work without a captured segment.

Routing::Intercepting routes.summary: Intercepting routes render a destination inside the current layout, preserving the user's context for patterns such as photo modals. Direct visits and refreshes render the full destination page instead.
Routing::Intercepting routes.explanation: An intercepting route lets navigation render a route from another part of the app inside the current layout, so a detail view can overlay its originating page. The browser keeps the originating context during client navigation, but a direct URL visit or refresh renders the full destination page instead.

example.title: Intercept a photo as a modal route
example.code:
app/
├── feed/
│   ├── page.tsx
│   └── (..)photo/[id]/page.tsx
└── photo/[id]/page.tsx
example.explanation: Place the intercepted page in a route group that matches the target segment from the feed context, while keeping the canonical photo page for direct visits and refreshes.

useCases.title: Photo preview modal
useCases.scenario: A user selects a photo from a feed.

useCases.title: Context-preserving details
useCases.scenario: A list item opens a detail view without losing the list context.

useCases.title: Shareable modal navigation
useCases.scenario: An application needs overlays while keeping destinations directly shareable.
